{{short description|Conditions under which the congruence x^3 equals p (mod q) is solvable}}
'''Cubic reciprocity''' is a collection of theorems in [[Number theory#Elementary number theory|elementary]] and [[algebraic number theory|algebraic]]  [[number theory]] that state conditions under which the [[Modular arithmetic|congruence]] ''x''<sup>3</sup>&nbsp;≡&nbsp;''p''&nbsp;(mod&nbsp;''q'') is solvable; the word "reciprocity" comes from the form of the [[#Statement of the theorem|main theorem]], which states that if ''p'' and ''q'' are primary numbers in the ring of [[Eisenstein integer]]s, both coprime to 3, the congruence ''x''<sup>3</sup> ≡ ''p'' (mod ''q'') is solvable if and only if  ''x''<sup>3</sup> ≡ ''q'' (mod ''p'') is solvable.

==History==

Sometime before 1748 [[Leonhard Euler|Euler]] made the first conjectures about the cubic residuacity of small integers, but they were not published until 1849, 62 years after his death.<ref>Euler, ''Tractatus ...'', §§ 407&ndash;410</ref>

Gauss's published works mention cubic residues and reciprocity three times: there is one result pertaining to cubic residues in the [[Disquisitiones Arithmeticae]] (1801).<ref>Gauss, DA, footnote to  art. 358</ref> In the introduction to the fifth and sixth [[proofs of quadratic reciprocity]] (1818)<ref>Gauss, ''Theorematis fundamentalis ...''</ref> he said that he was publishing these proofs because their techniques ([[Gauss's lemma (number theory)|Gauss's lemma]] and [[Quadratic Gauss sum|Gaussian sums]], respectively) can be applied to cubic and biquadratic reciprocity. Finally, a footnote in the second (of two) monographs on [[biquadratic reciprocity]] (1832) states that cubic reciprocity is most easily described in the ring of Eisenstein integers.<ref>Gauss, BQ, § 30</ref>

From his diary and other unpublished sources, it appears that Gauss knew the rules for the cubic and quartic residuacity of integers by 1805, and discovered the full-blown theorems and proofs of cubic and biquadratic reciprocity around 1814.<ref>Cox, pp. 83&ndash;90</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, pp. 199&ndash;201, 222&ndash;224</ref> Proofs of these were found in his posthumous papers, but it is not clear if they are his or Eisenstein's.<ref name="Lemmermeyer">Lemmermeyer, p. 200</ref>

[[Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi|Jacobi]] published several theorems about cubic residuacity in 1827, but no proofs.<ref>Jacobi, ''De residuis cubicis ...''.</ref> In his Königsberg lectures of 1836&ndash;37 Jacobi presented proofs.<ref name="Lemmermeyer" /> The first published proofs were by Eisenstein (1844).<ref>Eisenstein, ''Beweis des Reciprocitätssatzes ...''</ref><ref>Eisenstein, ''Nachtrag zum cubischen...''</ref><ref>Eisenstein, ''Application de l'algèbre...''</ref>

==Integers==

A '''cubic residue''' (mod ''p'') is any number congruent to the third power of an integer (mod ''p''). If ''x''<sup>3</sup> ≡ ''a'' (mod ''p'') does not have an integer solution, ''a'' is a '''cubic nonresidue'''  (mod ''p'').<ref name="CfGauss">cf. Gauss, BQ § 2</ref>

Cubic residues are usually only defined in modulus ''n'' such that <math>\lambda(n)</math> (the [[Carmichael lambda function]] of ''n'') is divisible by 3, since for other integer ''n'', all residues are cubic residues.

As is often the case in number theory, it is easier to work modulo prime numbers, so in this section all moduli ''p'', ''q'', etc., are assumed to be positive odd primes.<ref name="CfGauss" />

We first note that if ''q'' ≡ 2 (mod 3) is a prime then every number is a cubic residue modulo ''q''. Let ''q'' = 3''n'' + 2; since 0 = 0<sup>3</sup> is obviously a cubic residue, assume ''x'' is not divisible by ''q''. Then by [[Fermat's little theorem]],

:<math>x^q \equiv x \pmod{q}, \qquad x^{q - 1} \equiv  1 \pmod{q}</math>

Multiplying the two congruences we have

:<math> x^{2q-1} \equiv x \pmod{q}</math>

Now substituting 3''n'' + 2 for ''q'' we have:

:<math> x^{2q-1} = x^{6n + 3} = \left  (x^{2n+1} \right )^3.</math>

Therefore, the only interesting case is when the modulus ''p'' ≡ 1 (mod 3). In this case the non-zero residue classes (mod ''p'') can be divided into three sets, each containing (''p''−1)/3 numbers. Let ''e'' be a cubic non-residue. The first set is the cubic residues; the second one is ''e'' times the numbers in the first set, and the third is ''e''<sup>2</sup> times the numbers in the first set. Another way to describe this division is to let ''e'' be a [[Primitive root modulo n|primitive root]] (mod ''p''); then the first (resp. second, third) set is the numbers whose indices with respect to this root are congruent to 0 (resp. 1, 2) (mod 3). In the vocabulary of [[group theory]], the cubic residues form a subgroup of [[Index of a subgroup|index]] 3 of the multiplicative group <math>(\Z/p\Z)^{\times}</math> and the three sets are its cosets.

===Primes ≡ 1 (mod 3)===

A theorem of Fermat<ref>Gauss, DA, Art. 182</ref><ref>Cox, Ex. 1.4&ndash;1.5</ref> states that every prime ''p'' ≡ 1 (mod 3) can be written as ''p'' = ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 3''b''<sup>2</sup> and (except for the signs of ''a'' and ''b'') this representation is unique.

Letting ''m'' = ''a'' + ''b'' and  ''n'' = ''a'' − ''b'', we see that this is equivalent to ''p'' = ''m''<sup>2</sup> − ''mn'' +  ''n''<sup>2</sup> (which equals (''n'' − ''m'')<sup>2</sup> − (''n'' − ''m'')''n'' + ''n''<sup>2</sup> = ''m''<sup>2</sup> + ''m''(''n'' − ''m'') + (''n'' − ''m'')<sup>2</sup>, so ''m'' and ''n'' are not determined uniquely). Thus,
:<math>\begin{align}
4p &= (2m-n)^2 + 3n^2 \\
&= (2n-m)^2 + 3m^2 \\
&= (m+n)^2 + 3(m-n)^2
\end{align}</math>
and it is a straightforward exercise to show that exactly one of ''m'', ''n'', or ''m'' − ''n'' is a multiple of 3, so

:<math>p = \frac14 (L^2+ 27M^2),</math>

and this representation is unique up to the signs of ''L'' and ''M''.<ref>Ireland & Rosen, Props 8.3.1 & 8.3.2</ref>

For relatively prime integers ''m'' and ''n'' define the '''rational cubic residue symbol''' as

:<math>\left[\frac{m}{n}\right]_3 = \begin{cases} 1  & m \text{ is a cubic residue } \pmod{n} \\ -1 & m \text{ is a cubic non-residue }\pmod{n} \end{cases}</math>

This symbol does ''not'' have the multiplicative properties of the Legendre symbol; for this, we need the true cubic character with values in the cubic roots of 1 defined below.

:'''Euler's conjectures (now proved).''' Let ''p'' = ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 3''b''<sup>2</sup> be a prime. Then the following hold:<ref>Euler, ''Tractatus'', §§ 407&ndash;401</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, p. 222&ndash;223<!--; an apparent misprint has been corrected (See Talk)--></ref><ref>''Tractatus de numerorum doctrina capita sedecim, quae supersunt'', '''411''', footnote (chapter 11) [http://eulerarchive.maa.org/pages/E792.html]</ref>
::<math>\begin{align}
\left[\tfrac{2}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad 3\mid b\\
\left[\tfrac{3}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad 9\mid b \text{ or } 9\mid(a\pm b)\\
\left[\tfrac{5}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad 15\mid b \text{ or } 3\mid b \text{ and } 5\mid a \text{ or } 15\mid(a\pm b) \text{ or } 15\mid(2a\pm b)\\
\left[\tfrac{6}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad 9\mid b \text{ or } 9\mid(a\pm 2b)\\
\left[\tfrac{7}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad (3\mid b\text{ and }7\mid a) \text{ or } 21\mid (b\pm a) \text{ or } 7\mid(4b\pm a) \text{ or } 21\mid b \text{ or } 7\mid(b\pm 2a)
\end{align}</math>

The first two can be restated as follows. Let ''p'' be a prime that is congruent to 1 modulo 3. Then:<ref>Cox, p. 2, Thm. 4.15, Ex. 4.15</ref><ref>Ireland & Rosen, Prop. 9.6.2, Ex 9.23</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, Prop. 7.1 & 7.2</ref>
* 2 is a cubic residue of ''p'' if and only if ''p'' = ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 27''b''<sup>2</sup>.
* 3 is a cubic residue of ''p'' if and only if 4''p'' = ''a''<sup>2</sup> + 243''b''<sup>2</sup>.

:'''Gauss's theorem.''' Let ''p'' be a positive prime such that
::<math>p = 3n + 1= \tfrac14 \left(L^2+ 27M^2\right).</math> 
:Then <math> L(n!)^3\equiv 1 \pmod{p}.</math><ref>Gauss, DA footnote to art. 358</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, Ex. 7.9</ref>

One can easily see that Gauss's Theorem implies:
:<math>\left[\tfrac{L}{p}\right]_3 = \left[\tfrac{M}{p}\right]_3 =1.</math>

:'''Jacobi's theorem (stated without proof).'''<ref>Jacobi, ''De residuis cubicis...''</ref> Let ''q'' ≡ ''p'' ≡ 1 (mod 6) be positive primes. Obviously both ''p'' and ''q'' are also congruent to 1 modulo 3, therefore assume: 
::<math>p = \tfrac14 \left(L^2+ 27M^2\right), \qquad q = \tfrac14 \left(L'^2+ 27M'^2\right).</math> 
:Let ''x'' be a solution of ''x''<sup>2</sup> ≡ −3 (mod ''q''). Then
::<math>x\equiv\pm \frac{L'}{3M'}\pmod{q},</math>
:and we have:
::<math>\begin{align}
\left[\frac{q}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad \left[\frac{\frac{L+3Mx}{2}p}{q}\right]_3 =1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \left[\frac{\frac{L+3Mx}{L-3Mx}}{q}\right]_3 =1 \\
\left[\frac{q}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longrightarrow \quad \left[\frac{\frac{LM'+L'M}{LM'-L'M}}{q}\right]_3 =1
\end{align}</math>

:'''[[Emma Lehmer|Lehmer]]'s Theorem.''' Let ''q'' and ''p'' be primes, with <math>p = \tfrac14 \left(L^2+ 27M^2\right).</math> Then:<ref>Lemmermeyer, Prop.7.4</ref>
::<math>\left[\frac{q}{p}\right]_3 = 1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad q \mid LM \text{ or } L\equiv\pm \frac{9r}{2u+1} M\pmod{q},</math>
:where 
::<math>u\not\equiv 0,1,-\tfrac12, -\tfrac13 \pmod{q} \quad  \text{and} \quad 3u+1 \equiv r^2 (3u-3)\pmod{q}.</math>

Note that the first condition implies that any number that divides ''L'' or ''M'' is a cubic residue (mod ''p'').

The first few examples<ref>Lemmermeyer, pp. 209&ndash;212, Props 7.1–7.3</ref> of this are equivalent to Euler's conjectures:

:<math>\begin{align}
\left[\frac{2}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad L \equiv M \equiv 0 \pmod{2} \\
\left[\frac{3}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad M \equiv 0 \pmod{3} \\
\left[\frac{5}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad LM \equiv 0 \pmod{5} \\
\left[\frac{7}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad &\Longleftrightarrow \quad LM \equiv 0 \pmod{7}
\end{align}</math>
<!--
Lemmermeyer says:
\left[\frac{11}{p}\right]_3 =1 &\text{ if and only if } &LM(L-3M)(L+3M) &\equiv 0 \pmod{11} \\
\left[\frac{13}{p}\right]_3 =1 &\text{ if and only if } &LM(L-2M)(L+2M) &\equiv 0 \pmod{13}
The correct versions seem:
\left[\frac{11}{p}\right]_3 =1 &\text{ if and only if } &LM(L-4M)(L+4M) &\equiv 0 \pmod{11} \\
\left[\frac{13}{p}\right]_3 =1 &\text{ if and only if } &LM(L-M)(L+M) &\equiv 0 \pmod{13}

-->
Since obviously ''L'' ≡ ''M'' (mod 2), the criterion for ''q'' = 2 can be simplified as:
:<math> \left[\frac{2}{p}\right]_3 =1 \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad M \equiv 0 \pmod{2}. </math>

:'''Martinet's theorem.''' Let ''p'' ≡ ''q'' ≡ 1 (mod 3) be primes, <math> pq = \tfrac14 (L^2 + 27 M^2).</math> Then<ref>Lemmermeyer, Ex. 7.11</ref>
::<math>\left[\frac{L}{p}\right]_3 \left[\frac{L}{q}\right]_3 =1\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad \left[\frac{q}{p}\right]_3  \left[\frac{p}{q}\right]_3 =1.</math>

:'''Sharifi's theorem.''' Let ''p''  = 1 + 3''x'' + 9''x''<sup>2</sup> be a prime. Then any divisor of ''x'' is a cubic residue (mod ''p'').<ref>Lemmermeyer, Ex. 7.12</ref>

==Eisenstein integers==

===Background===

In his second monograph on biquadratic reciprocity, Gauss says:

<blockquote>The theorems on biquadratic residues gleam with the greatest simplicity and genuine beauty only when the field of arithmetic is extended to '''imaginary''' numbers, so that without restriction, the numbers of the form ''a'' + ''bi'' constitute the object of study ... we call such numbers '''integral complex numbers'''.<ref>Gauss, BQ, § 30, translation in Cox, p. 83</ref> [bold in the original]</blockquote>

These numbers are now called the [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of [[Gaussian integers]], denoted by '''Z'''[''i'']. Note that ''i'' is a fourth root of 1.

In a footnote he adds

<blockquote>The theory of cubic residues must be based in a similar way on a consideration of numbers of the form ''a'' + ''bh'' where ''h'' is an imaginary root of the equation ''h''<sup>3</sup> = 1 ... and similarly the theory of residues of higher powers leads to the introduction of other imaginary quantities.<ref>Gauss, BQ, § 30, translation in Cox, p. 84</ref></blockquote>

In his first monograph on cubic reciprocity<ref>Ireland & Rosen p. 14</ref> Eisenstein developed the theory of the numbers built up from a cube [[root of unity]]; they are now  called the ring of [[Eisenstein integers]]. Eisenstein said that to investigate the properties of this ring one need only consult Gauss's work on '''Z'''[''i''] and modify the proofs. This is not surprising since both rings are [[unique factorization domain]]s.

The "other imaginary quantities" needed for the "theory of residues of higher powers" are the [[Ring of integers|rings of integers]] of the [[Cyclotomic field|cyclotomic number field]]s; the Gaussian and Eisenstein integers are the simplest examples of these.

===Facts and terminology===

Let

:<math>\omega = \frac{-1 + i\sqrt 3}{2} = e^\frac{2\pi i}{3}, \qquad \omega^3 = 1.</math>

And consider the ring of [[Eisenstein integer]]s:

:<math>\Z[\omega] = \left \{ a + b \omega  \ : \ a, b \in \Z \right \}.</math>

This is a [[Euclidean domain]] with the [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] function given by:

:<math>N(a + b \omega) = a^2 -ab + b^2.</math>

Note that the norm is always congruent to 0 or 1 (mod 3).

The [[group of units]] in <math>\Z[\omega]</math> (the elements with a [[multiplicative inverse]] or equivalently those with unit norm) is a [[cyclic group]] of the sixth roots of unity,

:<math>\left \{ \pm 1, \pm \omega, \pm \omega^2\right \}.</math>

<math>\Z[\omega]</math> is a [[unique factorization domain]]. The primes fall into three classes:<ref>Ireland & Rosen Prop 9.1.4</ref>

* 3 is a special case: 
::<math> 3 = -\omega^2 (1-\omega)^2.</math>
:It is the only prime in <math>\Z</math> divisible by the square of a prime in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>. The prime 3 is said to [[splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions|ramify]] in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>.

* Positive primes in <math>\Z</math> congruent to 2 (mod 3) are also primes in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>. These primes are said to remain [[splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions|inert]] in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>. Note that if <math>q</math> is any inert prime then:
::<math>N(q) = q^2 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}.</math>

* Positive primes in <math>\Z</math> congruent to 1 (mod 3) are the product of two conjugate primes in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>. These primes are said to [[splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions|split]] in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>. Their factorization is given by:
::<math>p=N (\pi) = N (\overline{\pi})= \pi  \overline{\pi}.</math> 
:for example
::<math> 7 = ( 3 + \omega) ( 2 - \omega).</math>

A number is '''primary''' if it is coprime to 3 and congruent to an ordinary integer modulo <math>(1-\omega)^2,</math> which is the same as saying it is congruent to <math>\pm 2</math> modulo 3. If <math>\gcd(N(\lambda), 3) = 1</math> one of <math>\lambda, \omega \lambda,</math> or <math>\omega^2 \lambda</math> is primary. Moreover, the product of two primary numbers is primary and the conjugate of a primary number is also primary.

The unique factorization theorem for <math>\Z[\omega]</math> is: if <math>\lambda \neq 0,</math> then
:<math>\lambda = \pm\omega^\mu(1-\omega)^\nu\pi_1^{\alpha_1}\pi_2^{\alpha_2}\pi_3^{\alpha_3} \cdots, \qquad \mu \in \{0, 1, 2\}, \quad \nu, \alpha_1, \alpha_2, \ldots \geqslant 0</math>
where each <math>\pi_i</math> is a primary (under Eisenstein's definition) prime. And this representation is unique, up to the order of the factors.

The notions of [[Modular arithmetic|congruence]]<ref>cf. Gauss, BQ, §§ 38&ndash;45</ref> and [[greatest common divisor]]<ref>cf. Gauss, BQ, §§ 46&ndash;47</ref> are defined the same way in <math>\Z[\omega]</math> as they are for the ordinary integers <math>\Z</math>. Because the units divide all numbers, a congruence modulo <math>\lambda</math> is also true modulo any associate of <math>\lambda</math>, and any associate of a GCD is also a GCD.

===Cubic residue character===

====Definition====
An analogue of [[Fermat's little theorem]] is true in <math>\Z[\omega]</math>: if <math>\alpha</math> is not divisible by a prime <math>\pi</math>,<ref>Ireland & Rosen. Prop. 9.3.1</ref>

:<math>\alpha^{N (\pi) - 1} \equiv 1 \pmod{\pi}.</math>

Now assume that <math>N(\pi) \neq 3</math> so that <math>N(\pi) \equiv 1 \pmod{3}.</math> Or put differently <math>3\mid N(\pi) -1.</math> Then we can write:

:<math>\alpha^{\frac{N ( \pi )- 1}{3}}\equiv \omega^k \pmod{\pi}, </math>

for a unique unit <math>\omega^k.</math> This unit is called the '''cubic residue character''' of <math>\alpha</math> modulo <math>\pi</math> and is denoted by<ref>Ireland & Rosen, p. 112</ref> 
:<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\pi}\right)_3 = \omega^k  \equiv \alpha^{\frac{N(\pi) - 1}{3}} \pmod{\pi}.</math>

====Properties====
The cubic residue character has formal properties similar to those of the [[Legendre symbol]]:

* If <math>\alpha \equiv \beta \pmod{\pi}</math> then <math>\left (\tfrac{\alpha}{\pi}\right )_3=\left (\tfrac{\beta}{\pi}\right )_3.</math>
* <math>\left (\tfrac{\alpha\beta}{\pi}\right )_3=\left (\tfrac{\alpha}{\pi}\right )_3\left (\tfrac{\beta}{\pi}\right )_3.</math>
* <math>\overline{\left (\tfrac{\alpha}{\pi}\right )_3}=\left (\tfrac{\overline{\alpha}}{\overline{\pi}}\right )_3,</math> where the bar denotes [[Complex conjugate|complex conjugation]].
* If <math>\pi</math> and <math>\theta</math> are associates then <math>\left (\tfrac{\alpha}{\pi}\right )_3=\left (\tfrac{\alpha}{\theta}\right )_3</math>
* The congruence <math>x^3 \equiv \alpha \pmod{\pi}</math> has a solution in <math>\Z[\omega]</math> if and only if <math>\left(\tfrac{\alpha}{\pi}\right)_3 = 1.</math><ref>Ireland & Rosen, Prop. 9.3.3</ref>
* If <math>a, b \in \Z</math> are such that <math>\gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, 3) = 1,</math> then <math>\left(\tfrac{a}{b}\right)_3 = 1.</math><ref>Ireland & Rosen, Prop. 9.3.4</ref><ref>Lemmermeyer, Prop 7.7</ref>
* The cubic character can be extended multiplicatively to composite numbers (coprime to 3) in the "denominator" in the same way the Legendre symbol is generalized into the [[Jacobi symbol]]. As with the Jacobi symbol, this extension sacrifices the "numerator is a cubic residue mod the denominator" meaning: the symbol is still guaranteed to be 1 when the "numerator" is a cubic residue, but the converse no longer holds.
::<math>\left(\frac{\alpha}{\lambda}\right)_3 = \left(\frac{\alpha}{\pi_1}\right)_3^{\alpha_1} \left(\frac{\alpha}{\pi_2}\right)_3^{\alpha_2} \cdots,</math>
:where 
::<math>\lambda = \pi_1^{\alpha_1}\pi_2^{\alpha_2}\pi_3^{\alpha_3} \cdots</math>

===Statement of the theorem===

Let &alpha; and &beta; be primary. Then

:<math>\Bigg(\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\Bigg)_3 = \Bigg(\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\Bigg)_3. </math>

There are supplementary theorems<ref>Lemmermeyer, Th. 6.9</ref><ref>Ireland & Rosen, Ex. 9.32&ndash;9.37</ref> for the units and the prime 1 − &omega;:

Let &alpha; = ''a'' + ''b''&omega; be primary, ''a'' = 3''m'' + 1 and ''b'' = 3''n''. (If ''a'' ≡ 2 (mod 3) replace &alpha; with its associate −&alpha;; this will not change the value of the cubic characters.) Then

:<math>
\Bigg(\frac{\omega}{\alpha}\Bigg)_3 = \omega^\frac{1-a-b}{3}= \omega^{-m-n},\;\;\;
\Bigg(\frac{1-\omega}{\alpha}\Bigg)_3 = \omega^\frac{a-1}{3}= \omega^m,\;\;\;
\Bigg(\frac{3}{\alpha}\Bigg)_3 = \omega^\frac{b}{3}= \omega^n.
</math>

<!--Along the same lines, von Lienen proved<ref>Lemmermeyer, p. 226&ndash;227</ref>

:<math>\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)_3 \left(\frac{q}{p}\right)_3  = \left(\frac{\frac{L'M+LM'}{2M}}{p}\right)_3^2.</math>

In this expression, the definition of <math>\left(\tfrac{p}{q}\right)_3</math> is different from the one used elsewhere. To explain this, we split <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> into <math>p = \pi\overline{\pi}, q = \rho\overline{\rho},</math> where <math>\pi, \overline{\pi}, \rho, \overline{\rho}</math> are [[Eisenstein prime]]s congruent to 2 modulo 3 that satisfy

:<math> \rho \equiv \tfrac{N}{2M} \pmod{\pi}, \quad \pi \equiv \tfrac{N}{2M'} \pmod{\rho}, \quad N = L'M + LM', \quad L \equiv L'\equiv 1 \pmod{3}.</math>

Von Lienen defined

:<math>\left(\tfrac{p}{q}\right)_3 := \chi_{\rho}(p),</math>

where <math>\chi_{\rho}</math> denotes a cubic residue character modulo <math>\rho</math> (see [[#Cubic residue character|below]]).  Note that the value of <math>\text{Li}(p,q) = \left(\tfrac{p}{q}\right)_3</math> is not uniquely determined. For example, when <math>p = \alpha\overline{\alpha}</math> satisfies the above conditions, one can choose either <math>\alpha</math> or <math>\overline{\alpha}</math> and call it <math>\pi.</math> However, once <math>\pi</math> is chosen, <math>\rho</math> is uniquely determined, and both <math>\text{Li}(x,q)</math> and <math>\text{Li}(x,p)</math> are unambiguously defined for any <math>x.</math>

  | last1 = Euler | first1 = Leonhard
  | title = Opera Omnia, Series prima, Vols I&ndash;V
  | publisher = Teubner
  | location = Leipzig & Berlin
  | date = 1911–1944}}

===Gauss===

The two monographs Gauss published on biquadratic reciprocity have consecutively numbered sections: the first contains §§ 1&ndash;23 and the second §§ 24&ndash;76. Footnotes referencing these are of the form "Gauss, BQ, § ''n''". Footnotes referencing the ''Disquisitiones Arithmeticae'' are of the form "Gauss, DA, Art. ''n''".

*{{citation
  | last1 = Gauss  | first1 = Carl Friedrich
  | title = Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, Commentatio prima
  | publisher = Comment. Soc. regiae sci, Göttingen 6
  | location = Göttingen
  | date = 1828}}

*{{citation
  | last1 = Gauss  | first1 = Carl Friedrich
  | title = Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, Commentatio secunda
  | publisher = Comment. Soc. regiae sci, Göttingen 7
  | location = Göttingen
  | date = 1832}}

These are in Gauss's ''Werke'', Vol II, pp.&nbsp;65&ndash;92 and 93&ndash;148

Gauss's fifth and sixth proofs of quadratic reciprocity are in

*{{citation
  | last1 = Gauss  | first1 = Carl Friedrich
  | title = Theoramatis fundamentalis in doctrina de residuis quadraticis demonstrationes et amplicationes novae 
    | date = 1818}}

This is in Gauss's ''Werke'', Vol II, pp.&nbsp;47&ndash;64

German translations of all three of the above are the following, which also has the [[Disquisitiones Arithmeticae]] and Gauss's other papers on number theory.

*{{citation
  | last = Gauss  | first = Carl Friedrich
  | translator-last = Maser | translator-first = H. 
  | title = Untersuchungen uber hohere Arithmetik (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae & other papers on number theory) (Second edition)
  | publisher = Chelsea
  | location = New York
  | date = 1965
  | isbn = 0-8284-0191-8}}
